Right — and that's exactly why you *shouldn't* be the one to correct him. Not tonight, not in the lobby, not with a headset on. If you walk out there mid-preshow to litigate anything with a guy who's already got the Morrisons' ear, you look like the drama and he looks like the reasonable one who "just came to support the show." He wins that scene by default.

Here's what actually helps in the next 20 minutes:

- **Text whoever owns the donor relationship** — ED, board chair, development person, whoever. One line: "Heads up, Dennis is here and talking to the Morrisons in the lobby. Might be worth a follow-up call this week." That's it. You're not asking them to swoop in, you're making sure the right person knows to get the real version in front of the donors *later*, calmly, on the phone. Donors don't decide anything in a lobby. They decide after the calls.
- **Don't engage him.** If he tries to catch your eye or wave, you're busy. You are, in fact, busy.
- **Run a clean show.** I know that sounds like a poster in a green room, but the Morrisons are about to sit down and watch the thing *you're* running. That's the most persuasive counter-narrative available to you tonight and it doesn't require you to say a word.

The part that stings is that you can see the whole thing happening and can't touch it. That's a genuinely rotten place to be stuck for 90 minutes. But the version where you fix this is not "I stood up to Dennis in the lobby" — it's "he had a nice chat with the Morrisons, and then a week later the people who actually make decisions had a very different, much better-documented chat with them."

Let him work the room. You work the board. Then take a breath and call places when you're out.

You're right that I'm not seeing it, so I'll take your read: he's campaigning, it's landing, and it's happening in your house on your night. That's infuriating. Let's still be careful about the frame, because the frame is the thing that'll bite you later.

**"Why did you let him campaign in the lobby" is a trap question, and you don't have to accept the premise.** You didn't *let* anything. A person bought a ticket to a public performance. Unless there's a formal no-contact situation or a trespass order, there is no version of tonight where a stage manager (or anyone) can bar a ticketholder from talking to other ticketholders. A board that's worth anything knows this. If someone asks it anyway, your answer is short and boring:

> "He bought a ticket. It's a public show. I flagged it to [name] the moment I saw him with the Morrisons, and I ran the show. The follow-up with the Morrisons is on the development side, and it should happen this week."

That's it. That answer makes *you* the calm professional and quietly points at who actually owns the next move. The one thing that would make you look bad is if the board hears about this from Dennis, the Morrisons, or the grapevine before they hear it from you. So:

- **Send the heads-up text now if you haven't.** ED or board chair, one or two lines, timestamped. That's your receipt. You saw it, you escalated it, you didn't make a scene. Done.
- **Have the "what he's saying" conversation tomorrow, not tonight.** If the Morrisons got a version of events, the counter is a phone call from someone with standing, with the actual record in hand, *not* a stage manager buttonholing them at intermission.

Laughing donors in a lobby feel like a verdict. They're not. People laugh with whoever's standing in front of them holding a wine. What sticks is who calls them Tuesday with a clear, calm story and a plan. Make sure that's your side, and make sure the board hears from you first.

Now go call your places — that's the thing tonight that only you can do.

Text them: "Dennis is working the Morrisons by the bar. Can you go say hi to the Morrisons?" Not confront Dennis. Just... show up. **Board chair's wife being here is good for you, not bad.** She's about to see exactly what you're seeing: a guy who got benched, showing up on opening night and working donors. Nobody looks at that and thinks "what a gracious supporter." She's going to go home and tell the chair, and now the chair has your text *and* an eyewitness. You don't have to narrate it for anyone. It narrates itself.

**Actors' families don't care about Dennis.** They're here for their kid. Whatever he's saying, they're going to forget it the second the lights go down, and they'll remember the show.

On the "rewriting the story in real time" feeling: I know it feels like the record is being written out there. But a lobby chat has a half-life of about a glass of wine. The things that actually stick are written down, dated, and told by people with standing, and you've already got one of those in motion. His pitch tonight is loud and disappears. Your text is quiet and stays.

So: one more text to whoever can be in that lobby, then you're genuinely done with the part you can control. Running the show isn't "smiling and running the lights." It's the reason the Morrisons wrote the check in the first place. Go do the part he can't.
